analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate tax and cuts the top gift tax rate to 35%.
analysis.headline: The House passed the estate tax repeal 240-179 on April 16, 2015, but the Senate never took it up, and it died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The federal estate tax is a tax on very large inheritances, paid only by estates above an exemption threshold (about $5.4 million per person in 2015). This bill would have repealed that tax and the related generation-skipping transfer tax entirely, and cut the top gift tax rate from 40% to 35%. The House passed it with nearly every Republican voting yes, but the Senate never voted on it, and it expired when the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to the largest estates in the country. Because the tax only applies above roughly $5.4 million per person in exemptions, the benefit goes to a small share of very wealthy families; everyone else's estate was already below the threshold.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the estate tax and generation-skipping transfer tax for anyone dying or transferring assets on or after enactment, so heirs of large estates would owe nothing on the inheritance.
Lowers the top gift tax rate to 35%, down from 40%, making it cheaper to move large wealth during life.
Sets the lifetime gift exemption at $5 million with inflation adjustments ($5.43 million in 2015), while closing one loophole by treating certain transfers in trust as taxable gifts.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally. The estate tax is a source of federal revenue, and repealing it would mean the money comes from somewhere else or adds to deficits; the bill exempts its budgetary effects from statutory pay-as-you-go enforcement, so its cost would not trigger automatic spending cuts.

drawbacks.text: The estate tax applies only to the largest estates, so repeal concentrates a revenue loss on the general Treasury while the benefit goes to a small number of wealthy families.
Section 4 exempts the bill's budgetary effects from the pay-as-you-go scorecards, meaning the bill's cost to the Treasury would not trigger automatic budget enforcement.

A good-faith objection from supporters was that heirs to family farms and small businesses sometimes faced the tax; however, the bill offered no targeted relief for them, instead repealing the tax for the largest estates across the board.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but narrow: only heirs of estates above the roughly $5.4 million exemption would have paid less. The cost is a permanent loss of federal revenue spread across everyone else, and the bill structured itself to bypass the budget rules that would normally force Congress to account for that cost.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it in April 2015, but the Senate received the bill and never voted on it, so it expired when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: The Ways and Means Committee reported the bill 22-10 in March 2015.

On April 16, 2015, Rep. Nolan moved to recommit the bill with instructions to add a section disallowing tax benefits in cases of gift and estate tax evasion; the motion failed 186-232, with 232 of 243 Republicans voting no.
The House passed the bill 240-179 on April 16, 2015, with 233 of 243 Republicans in favor and 176 of 188 Democrats opposed.
The Senate received the bill on April 20, 2015, and no further action was ever taken.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never became law, the federal estate tax continued to apply to the largest estates, and the Treasury kept that revenue. The families and heirs who would have benefited from repeal gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Treasury; the tax stayed in place

industries.industry: Heirs and family dynasties of the largest estates
industries.note: Repeal would have let the wealthiest families pass full estates to heirs tax-free, while the lost revenue would fall on the general Treasury. Only estates above the roughly $5.4 million exemption had ever owed the tax.
A large part of this industry's work exists to navigate the estate tax; repeal would have shrunk that market. Their loss would have coincided with the public keeping the revenue.
